1:
Whether the Egyptian marriage was a sin is the chapter's sharpest question, and Clarke and Ellicott answer it flatly against each other. Clarke grants the politics, that it strengthened the kingdom as the alliance with Tyre did, then asks whether politics should prevail over express laws of God; he quotes the law forbidding Israel to give daughters to or take daughters from such nations, holds that Solomon acted in direct opposition to it, and suggests that in it were sown the seeds of the apostasy in which he so long lived and so awfully died. He sets out the apologists' case in four points, that the bride must have been a proselyte, that God was not displeased, that the Song would not stand in the canon if its spouse were an idolatress, and that Solomon is nowhere blamed, and answers each. There is no evidence she was a proselyte, any more than that her father was a believer; if the law is positively against such matches God cannot have been pleased by one; the Song's place in the canon proves nothing on some critics' view of that book. And Solomon is expressly reproved, since Nehemiah asks whether he did not sin by these things, beloved of God though he was, and says outlandish women caused even him to sin; while the later chapter assigning the cause of his apostasy names the daughter of Pharaoh first among the strange women.

Ellicott finds no fault. The sacred historian, he observes, finds none either, the Egyptians never being regarded with the aversion felt towards the women of the Canaanite races; and since the marriage is nowhere connected with the later declension, it is not unlikely that the new queen literally did what the Psalmist calls for and forgot her own people and her father's house. He also supplies the setting that makes the match intelligible: Egypt appears from its own records to have been weak and divided under the Tanite dynasty of the lower kingdom, with Assyrian power in a corresponding abeyance, which gave scope for Israel's sudden rise and probably induced the Egyptian king to consent to an alliance earlier Pharaohs might have spurned. Gill asks a different question, why no Egyptian ruler is mentioned in Scripture between Moses and this point, when the kingdom was powerful and near; and answers from Diodorus Siculus that the kings of that stretch had nothing worthy of relation. He canvasses two names, one heathen writer calling him Vaphres and reporting letters still preserved between him and Solomon about workmen for the temple, while Calvisius thought him Sesostris.

On the high places Ellicott does the chapter's most careful work. The historian writes from his own later standpoint, when worship at them had been forbidden, and explains the practice by the fact that no house was yet built. Two kinds must be distinguished: places of sacrifice to false gods, absolute abominations, and unauthorised sanctuaries of the Lord himself, which probably associated his worship with visible representations. The prohibition of the second kind had two objects, to guard against local corruptions of God's service and against worshipping him under visible forms, and to prevent a breach of national unity by the tribes gathering round separate sanctuaries; and it served a third besides, as a remarkable spiritual education for the worship of an invisible God without local emblems, preparatory to the perfect spirituality of the future. He adds that up to this time even under Samuel and David sacrifice away from the tabernacle was used without scruple, though alien from the spirit of the law. Gill locates the practice concretely, on the tops of houses and on hills and particularly at Gibeon, where the tabernacle then stood; and on Gibeon Ellicott notes that the name means belonging to a hill, which fixes it on the central plateau in Benjamin, while Gill puts it four or five miles from Jerusalem.
5:
What kind of dream this was gets three incompatible answers. Gill maximises it: not a common natural dream but a prophetic night vision of the sort God used with his prophets, in which Solomon had the full use of his reasoning powers and in the exercise of grace; and the Lord really did appear while he slept, by some display of his glory, not merely in a dream. Clarke naturalises it and then takes most of it back. It came the night after the sacrifices and probably after earnest prayer for wisdom, so the dream may have followed the prayer, the images that occupy the mind by day recurring at night. But probably, he concludes, we need not carry the matter so far into miracle. God might be the author of the extraordinary wisdom as he was of the riches; and that Solomon lay down ignorant and rose wiser than all the children of men is to Clarke as credible as that he lay down with a scanty revenue and woke to find his treasury full. God gave the seeds of an extraordinary understanding, and by much study they grew up under the divine blessing and produced a plentiful harvest; but alas, he adds, they did not continue to grow.

Ellicott reads the dream institutionally, as a symptom rather than a favour. Direct communication of this kind contrasts with David's indirect knowledge of God's will through Nathan and Gad and through the priest, and is perhaps the first sign of an abeyance of the prophetic office and a loss of leadership in the priesthood. He adds that the vision by dream is of a lower type than the waking vision, and is mostly recorded of men outside the covenant, of the early stages of revelation, and of the lapse of the prophetic succession during the captivity.

On what was asked for all three agree with different emphases. Gill says it was understanding not spiritual or natural, though both were given, but political, that he might rule Israel well; Clarke says he did not ask wisdom in general but the true science of government; Ellicott calls it the wisdom of the ruler, to discern and do true justice between man and man, and notes that Solomon looks for it as an inspiration of God rather than a fruit of experience. Ellicott reports his age variously estimated from twelve to twenty, and Clarke glosses the not knowing how to go out or come in as an infant learning to walk. Gill explains why it pleased God, that Solomon had respect not to his own advantage but to the people's good and God's honour.

Where the two part company is on how much of the promise was kept. Ellicott is precise: only one point, length of days, was conditional, and that one was not fulfilled, since the reign is given as forty years and his age could hardly have exceeded sixty, though Josephus, amplifying as usual, stretches the reign to eighty. The rest, he holds, received an extraordinary fulfilment, so that for the first and last time the monarchy assumed something of the character of an empire. Clarke questions the fulfilment far more deeply, asking whether the whole was not conditional, whether Solomon ever received all this wisdom, and whether his unfaithfulness did not prevent the divine purpose; for instead of being the wisest of men did he not become more brutish than any, worshipping abominations, itself a proof of the grossest stupidity. No character in the sacred writings, he says, disappoints us more. Gill keeps to what the waking showed, that Solomon knew the dream true at once, finding himself possessed of a wisdom he had never had; and Ellicott notes that he then stood before the ark in its tabernacle on Sion, a second and probably still more sacred place of worship, where the sacrifice is distinctly a thank-offering.
16:
What the two women were is disputed before anything else is, and Clarke rejects the English outright. The word our version renders harlots the Chaldee, which he calls the best judge in the case, renders tavern-keepers; and he adds three reasons. Harlots would hardly have dared appear before Solomon; common women would not likely have had children; and such persons would not have been permitted under the previous reign. The absence of any husband he explains by supposing them away about their necessary occupations, the case being too urgent to wait. Gill weighs the same question both ways and comes out differently. He reports the Targum making them victuallers or innkeepers, and gives the argument in their favour, that common prostitutes do not usually bear children, or if they do take no care of them and are not fond of them as these plainly were. But against that he sets the other evidence: no husbands are mentioned, they live together in one house and alone, and they are impudent and brawling and litigious, which gives great suspicion that the character our version gives them is the true one.

He also supplies the motive the text leaves out. When the other woman rose at midnight and perceived that she had overlaid her own child, she took no further care of it but resorted to the stratagem, either through fear of the punishment inflicted on such negligence or because of the disgrace of it.

The judgment itself draws the chapter's most interesting agreement, since both commentators who discuss it deny that it was miraculous. Ellicott calls it simply an instance of intuitive sagacity, cutting the knot of a hopeless difficulty by an appeal to maternal instinct, an appeal which might have failed but was the only one possible. It is in knowing how to risk failure rather than be reduced to impotence, he says, and how to go straight to the heart of a difficulty when the slow regular approaches of science are impossible, that men recognise a touch of genius, and that Scripture here recognises the wisdom of God. Clarke gets there more plainly. The decision was apparently very strange, and nothing could have vindicated it had it been carried into execution; but Solomon saw that the real mother would relinquish her claim rather than watch the child hewn in pieces, while the pretender would probably see it with indifference. The plan was tried and it succeeded, which Clarke calls a proof of sound judgment, penetration and acquaintance with human nature; but surely, he adds, it is not produced as a proof of extraordinary and supernatural wisdom.

Clarke then supports that deflation with a parallel from outside Scripture, and his handling of it is a small lesson in sourcing. Ariopharnes, appointed to decide among three young men who each claimed to be the dead king's son and heir, commanded each to shoot an arrow into the body of the deceased; two did it without hesitation, the third refused, and he was judged the son. The case, Clarke observes, works by a covert appeal to affection, exactly as the judgment here does. And he is scrupulous: Grotius cites the story from Diodorus Siculus, and Clarke says plainly that he reports it on that authority and has not himself been able to find the place in Diodorus.

At the close Clarke reads the people's fear as the measure of the decision. It proved to them that they could not impose upon the king, so that they were afraid to do what might bring them before his seat of judgment; and they saw the wisdom of God in him because they perceived that he was taught of God, judged impartially and could not be deceived. What was done to the other woman we are not told, he adds, though justice certainly required that she be punished for her lies and her fraud.
